title: Half-life
examples: How does the half-life affect the amount of material left?
Can you calculate the remaining amount after a certain time?
What is the difference between half-life and the decay constant?

explain.say: The half-life is the time needed for half the amount to decay.

draw.text: Half-life: Time for half to decay

explain.say: If we start with one hundred grams, after one half-life, fifty grams remain.
After two half-lives, the original amount will have reduced to one quarter.
To find the time, we multiply the number of half-lives by the half-life period.
In dating, we measure the remaining radioactive material to find the age.
When calculating, always ensure your time units match the half-life unit.

items: Time unit must match half-life unit
Example: If half-life is years, time must be in years

faq.q: Does the half-life change depending on how much material is left?
faq.a: No, the half-life is constant for a specific radioactive isotope. It does not change based on the amount present.
asks: Does the starting mass affect the half-life?

faq.q: If the half-life is very long, does that mean it decays slowly?
faq.a: Yes, a very long half-life means the material decays very slowly over time. It takes a long time to reduce by half.
asks: What does a long half-life imply?
Does a big number mean slow decay?

faq.q: How do I use the formula to find the remaining fraction?
faq.a: You can use the formula amount remaining equals initial amount times two to the negative number of half-lives.
asks: How do I calculate the fraction left?

faq.q: Can we use half-life to date very old things like rocks?
faq.a: Yes, this process is called radiometric dating. Scientists measure the decay of known isotopes to estimate the object's age.

faq.q: If I calculate the time, should I use the initial amount?
faq.a: No, the initial amount is only needed if you are calculating the final mass. The time calculation only needs the half-life period.
asks: Do I need the starting mass for time?
Is the initial amount used in the time calculation?

facts: Half-life is the time required for half of a radioactive substance to decay.
The half-life period is unique to each radioactive isotope.
Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics, meaning the decay rate is proportional to the amount present.
Dating methods use the known half-lives of isotopes found in natural materials.

quiz.say: A sample has a half-life of ten years. If it starts with 100 grams, how much remains after thirty years?
quiz.why: Thirty years is three half-lives (30 divided by 10). So, 100 grams becomes 50, then 25, and finally 12.5 grams.

wrong.0: This assumes only two half-lives have passed, ignoring the full thirty years.
wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the remaining amount by subtracting 10 grams three times.
wrong.2: This only accounts for one half-life passing, ignoring the remaining time.

quiz.say: If an isotope has a half-life of one minute, how long will it take for the amount to reduce to one-eighth of its original amount?
quiz.why: To reduce to one-eighth, you must go through three half-lives (1/2 $\times$ 1/2 $\times$ 1/2 = 1/8). Three half-lives times one minute equals three minutes.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the half-life by the denominator of the fraction.
wrong.1: This only accounts for the first half-life, not the full reduction to one-eighth.
wrong.3: This might come from mistakenly using the formula for decay rate instead of counting half-lives.

quiz.say: In carbon dating, the half-life of Carbon-14 is used to determine the age of:
quiz.why: Carbon-14 is found in living things, so its decay helps scientists date organic materials like wood or bone.

wrong.1: Igneous rocks are formed from cooled magma and do not contain the necessary organic material for this dating method.
wrong.2: While gases can be measured, the dating technique specifically targets fixed organic samples.
wrong.3: Metals do not typically incorporate the radioactive isotopes needed for this specific dating technique.
